rationale: B wins by a hair because it finds one more usable trade lane without turning the launch into fantasy: "Airbnb plugs into Concur and Ramp, putting the stay inside the expense report" gives a spend-management reporter a concrete integration story to test. A is cleaner, but its refusal of "A vendor-competition angle asking why Concur and Ramp" throws away a viable plumbing angle because it framed the wrong tension. Both are well above launch-announcement mush; B gives the founder a slightly wider, still defensible pitching map.
gaps_in_A: "A vendor-competition angle asking why Concur and Ramp — rivals in expense software — both integrated with Airbnb — `no_journalist_shape`" is too quick to kill. The rivalry frame is weak, but the expense-stack integration frame has a real trade audience.
"hotel chains have used to lock in corporate travel budgets" is plausible industry context, but it is not in the update. That claim needs a source before it carries a pitch.

"business-trends reporter or a features desk" is the softest beat definition in the set. The angle gets sharper when aimed at travel-industry data or corporate-travel-policy reporters, not a generic trends desk.
gaps_in_B: "putting the stay inside the expense report" may overspecify the data flow. The update says direct integration with Concur and Ramp for expenses, not exactly what data lands where.
"a legacy expense system and a newer one" is outside knowledge, not supplied fact. It is useful color only if the pitch can prove why that pairing matters.
"rogue Airbnb bookings on personal cards" is a plausible pain point, but it is invented unless a travel manager confirms it.
"people who are often one-property operators" smuggles in a host-profile claim the update does not provide. Keep it as a question, not a premise.
